title: built its own CAD editor and then designed inside it. the demos i’ve seen are...
author: zhod
verification: Fetched from X via twitter-cli from global-search; original author and post URL preserved.
note: Original post did not expose a complete repeatable prompt. Treat this as a real showcase post, not a verified tutorial.
originalText:
Every few weeks it’s a new funeral.

> Artists are cooked. 
> Programmers are cooked.

and now, mechanical engineers.

It’s been less than 48 hours since Fable 5 dropped and people are already rawdogging it through Adam straight into Fusion.

- A working V8 in minutes.
- A full 747 from one prompt.

The model even built its own CAD editor and then designed inside it.

the demos i’ve seen are genuinely crazy, & the reactions have been the same.

but here’s what we miss every time we doom-market AI:

AI wasn’t built originally to replace anyone’s work but to genuinely amplify it.

what got automated here for example is the clicking: the repetitive edits, the grunt work across 40 files.

What didn’t get automated is the judgment: stress analysis, tolerances, certification, and real life working conditions.

Adam’s own founder has said they’re targeting the boring repetitive stuff, and not precisely for it to do the job better than its engineers.

So does leaning on it make you less technical?

Depends how you use it.

If you skip the thinking & let it carry you, you’d definitely lose the plot.

If we it to move faster on what we collectively already understand, we just get better.

The tool doesn’t get to decide which.

We do.

title: Minecraft-style game built with one prompt
author: David J.
verification: Fetched from X via twitter-cli from global-search; original author and post URL preserved.
note: Original post did not expose a complete repeatable prompt. Treat this as a real showcase post, not a verified tutorial.
originalText:
Claude Fable 5 might be the biggest thing to EVER happen in AI

In the first hours after launch, people:

- One-shot a full Minecraft clone in 20 minutes. Terrain, caves, ores, day/night.
- Built a complete Pokémon clone, 151 originals with sprites, stats and cries. 8,000 lines, one prompt.
- Fed it a McKinsey report and got back a document of the same quality.

( @VaibhavSisinty has a great running list ).

For three years we've used AI to answer questions but this one does the work itself.

Stripe gave it a fifty-million-line codebase to migrate, two months of work for a team. Done in a day.

I've spent years paying specialists a fortune for work this now does by the hour. The options traders, engineers and analysts you used to need a war chest to afford.

And Anthropic showed how far it really goes....

The unrestricted version was SO good at finding security flaws across the world's software that they refused to release it, handed it to the people guarding critical infrastructure, and gave everyone else a version with the dangerous parts walled off.

We're building toward an economy where software moves money on its own and settles deals with no human in the loop. That only stands up if the code underneath can't be broken, and we just got the most powerful tool ever made for finding what is.

Anthropic's line at launch was "point it at something that matters."

That's the whole game now.

The model is the same for everyone who signs up.

The edge was never the tool. It's taste, conviction, and knowing what's worth building.

What a time.
